alt: Paper 2 is a 2-hour written exam worth 80 marks and 33.3% of the A-level. Section A offers Culture and Identity, Families and Households, Health, or Work, Poverty and Welfare; Section B offers Beliefs in Society, Global Development, The Media, or Stratification and Differentiation. Each section is 40 marks of extended writing.
caption: One topic from each option, 40 marks of extended writing in each section.

alt: Science as an open belief system (Popper’s falsification, Merton’s four norms) compared with the Azande’s closed belief in the poison oracle, which explained away failures. Polanyi and Kuhn argue science can also defend itself.
caption: Open systems change with evidence; closed systems explain it away.

after: ## 2. Religion, social change and social stability
alt: Two columns. Durkheim, Malinowski, Parsons, Bellah, Marx and feminists see religion supporting stability. Weber, Bruce, Maduro, Bloch and Worsley show ways religion can help bring social change.
caption: A strong essay weighs the conservative-force view against evidence of religion driving change.

after: ## 2. Religion, social change and social stability
alt: A chain from the Calvinist belief in predestination, to anxiety about salvation, to hard work and ascetic saving as signs of being chosen, to the spirit of capitalism. Below are Weber’s comparison with Hinduism and Confucianism and Kautsky’s criticism.
caption: For Weber, Calvinist beliefs were one cause of the spirit of capitalism.

after: ## 3. Religious organisations and New Age movements
alt: A two-by-two grid from Wallis. Churches are respectable and uniquely legitimate, denominations respectable and pluralistic, sects deviant and uniquely legitimate, and cults deviant and pluralistic, each with its classic features.
caption: Wallis sorts religious organisations by self-image and public image.

after: ## 3. Religious organisations and New Age movements
alt: Wallis’s three types of new religious movement on a line: world-rejecting (such as the Unification Church), world-accommodating (such as neo-Pentecostalism) and world-affirming (such as Scientology). Below, three explanations of growth from Weber, Stark and Bainbridge, and Wilson.
caption: Not every NRM is a sect: Wallis distinguishes three relationships with the world.

alt: Two chains from Bruce. Cultural defence: a community under threat is united by religion. Cultural transition: religion helps migrants adjust, then declines as they integrate. Pryce, Modood and O’Beirne are used to evaluate them.
caption: Religion may defend a community, ease its transition, or become a source of identity.

after: ## 5. Religion in the contemporary world: secularisation and globalisation
alt: Bars show people in England and Wales describing themselves as Christian falling from 59.3% in 2011 to 46.2% in 2021, while no religion rose from 25.2% to 37.2%. Below, explanations of decline set against arguments that religion is changing rather than declining.
caption: Census figures show decline, but sociologists dispute what it means.
